title: Olanzapine and Alcohol: Zyprexa Risks, Timing, and Safety
excerpt: Can you drink on olanzapine (Zyprexa)? How alcohol stacks with its sedation and blood pressure drop, why timing doesn't help, the injection and combo forms, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on olanzapine (Zyprexa)? How alcohol stacks with its sedation and blood pressure drop, why timing doesn't help, and warning signs to watch.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** olanzapine (brand name Zyprexa) and alcohol are a combination to avoid. The Zyprexa medication guide tells patients not to drink while taking it, and the prescribing information notes that in testing, alcohol made olanzapine's drop in blood pressure on standing worse. Both slow down the brain, so together they stack drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and slowed reactions. With larger amounts that can turn into deep sedation and slowed breathing. Olanzapine also stays in your body for a long time, so you can't plan your way around the interaction by spacing out a drink and a dose. This guide explains why the two clash, what the label actually says, what the different forms of olanzapine mean for you, and the warning signs that need help right away.

**The quick rules:** Ask the person who prescribes your olanzapine before you drink anything at all, even one drink. Don't stop or skip doses so you can drink. Don't drive or do anything risky after combining them. Stand up slowly. And if someone who takes olanzapine has been drinking and is hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused, very hot, stiff, or has a seizure, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your prescriber before drinking on olanzapine**, and **call 911 or get emergency care if** someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, fainting, having a seizure, confused or agitated in a way that isn't normal for them, or has a high temperature with stiff muscles. In the US, Poison Control is available at **1-800-222-1222** if you're unsure whether a combination or an extra dose is dangerous. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text **988** (US).

## What Olanzapine (Zyprexa) Is and Why People Take It

Olanzapine is an atypical antipsychotic, sometimes called a second-generation antipsychotic. **Zyprexa** is the original brand name, and generic olanzapine is the same drug. In the US it's approved for schizophrenia and for bipolar I disorder, both for treating manic or mixed episodes and for keeping mood stable over the long term. Doctors also prescribe it off-label for other reasons, such as severe nausea during chemotherapy, agitation, and some cases of treatment-resistant depression or eating disorders.

It comes in several forms, and all of them carry the same core alcohol concern:

- **Zyprexa tablets and generic olanzapine tablets**, taken by mouth once a day.
- **Zyprexa Zydis**, a tablet that dissolves on the tongue. Same drug, different delivery.
- **Zyprexa IntraMuscular**, a short-acting injection used in hospitals for acute agitation.
- **Zyprexa Relprevv**, a long-acting injection given every two or four weeks.
- **Symbyax**, a capsule that combines olanzapine with fluoxetine (Prozac), used for bipolar depression and treatment-resistant depression.
- **Lybalvi**, a tablet that combines olanzapine with samidorphan, a drug added to reduce weight gain.

If you're searching "Zyprexa and alcohol," everything on this page applies to you. The brand name doesn't change the chemistry.

## How Olanzapine and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Olanzapine works by blocking several types of receptors, which are the docking points brain chemicals use to send signals. Its main mental health effect comes from blocking dopamine and serotonin receptors. But it also blocks a few others very strongly, and those side effects are where alcohol causes trouble.

**1. Histamine blocking, which causes sedation.** Olanzapine is a powerful blocker of the histamine H1 receptor, the same target that makes older allergy pills like Benadryl drowsy-making. That's a big reason olanzapine makes many people sleepy and hungry. Alcohol is also a sedative: it boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory signal (glutamate). When two different sedating effects stack, the result can be much stronger than either one alone. That shows up as heavy drowsiness, slurred speech, clumsiness, slowed reactions, and poor judgment.

**2. Alpha-1 blocking, which drops blood pressure when you stand.** Olanzapine blocks alpha-1 receptors, which help your blood vessels tighten when you stand up so blood doesn't pool in your legs. Blocking them can cause *orthostatic hypotension*, a sudden drop in blood pressure when you get up that makes you dizzy, lightheaded, or faint. Alcohol widens blood vessels and dehydrates you, which pushes in the same direction. This isn't a guess: the Zyprexa prescribing information reports that when people took alcohol with olanzapine in a study, the drop in blood pressure on standing got worse. That's why falls are one of the most practical risks of the combination, especially getting up in the night to use the bathroom.

**3. Anticholinergic effects, which affect heat, gut, and thinking.** Olanzapine has some anticholinergic activity, meaning it partly blocks acetylcholine, a chemical involved in sweating, digestion, and memory. That contributes to dry mouth, constipation, and a reduced ability to cool down. Alcohol dehydrates and can also cloud thinking, so the two together can make confusion and overheating more likely, particularly in hot weather or a crowded venue.

**4. Breathing.** Most of the time, the combination causes heavy sedation rather than dangerous breathing problems. But both substances slow the brain, and at larger amounts of alcohol, or when other sedatives are also involved, breathing can slow down. That is the emergency end of the spectrum, and it's the reason "sleep it off" is the wrong plan if someone on olanzapine has drunk a lot and is hard to wake.

What alcohol does *not* seem to do is change olanzapine's blood levels much. The prescribing information says a single dose of alcohol in a study didn't meaningfully change how olanzapine was processed. In other words, the interaction is mostly about two drugs adding their effects on the brain and blood pressure, not about one drug raising the level of the other.

## What the Zyprexa Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

Here's what the official documents say, in plain words:

- **The patient medication guide** tells people to avoid drinking alcohol while taking Zyprexa.
- **The prescribing information** says that because olanzapine acts mainly on the brain, it should be used with caution alongside other drugs that act on the brain and with alcohol, and it specifically reports that alcohol worsened olanzapine's orthostatic hypotension.
- **The driving and machinery warning** says olanzapine can impair judgment, thinking, and motor skills, and that people shouldn't drive or operate hazardous machinery until they know how it affects them. Alcohol makes each of those impairments worse.
- **Other label warnings** that matter when drinking include falls, problems regulating body temperature, a lowered seizure threshold, trouble swallowing, and metabolic changes (weight, blood sugar, and cholesterol). We cover each below.

Some prescribers do allow an occasional drink for a particular patient who is stable on a steady dose. That's an individual judgment based on your dose, your other medicines, your health, and why you take olanzapine. It's a conversation to have with them, not a rule you can apply from an article.

## Can You Drink on Olanzapine at All? The "Just One Drink" Question

This is the question most people actually want answered, so here's an honest take.

The official answer is to avoid alcohol. In real life, some people on olanzapine have an occasional drink, and some prescribers are comfortable with that for specific patients. If yours is, let them set the amount, and still never drink on an empty stomach, close to driving, or alongside other sedating substances.

A few things make "one drink" feel stronger than you'd expect on olanzapine:

- **You start out partly sedated.** Many people on olanzapine already feel slowed down or sleepy, especially in the first weeks or after a dose increase. A drink lands on top of that.
- **Dizziness on standing is more likely.** One drink can be enough to push a mild head rush into a fall.
- **Your usual limit no longer applies.** How you handled alcohol before starting olanzapine isn't a good guide to how you'll handle it now.
- **Other medicines change the picture.** If you also take a benzodiazepine (like Xanax or Klonopin), a sleep medicine, an opioid, gabapentin, or a sedating antihistamine, the risk climbs a lot.

If your prescriber hasn't said it's okay for you, the safe default is not to drink.

## Timing: How Long After Olanzapine Can You Drink, and Vice Versa?

People often ask whether they can take their dose in the morning and drink at night, or drink and then take their dose late. With olanzapine, that strategy doesn't work well, and the reason is its long half-life.

A drug's half-life is how long it takes your body to clear half of it. Olanzapine's half-life averages around 30 hours, and in some people it's longer than that. If you take it every day, your levels stay fairly steady around the clock. There isn't a "low point" in the day when olanzapine is gone and alcohol is safe.

The tablet's levels peak roughly six hours after a dose, so drinking in the hours after you take it lines up with its strongest effects. But even far from your dose, plenty of olanzapine is still in your system.

For the long-acting injection (Relprevv), timing matters even less. The drug is released slowly over weeks, so there's always a steady amount present between injections.

The bottom line on timing: spacing doesn't remove the interaction. If you're going to drink at all, the question is how much, not when, and that's for your prescriber to answer.

## Zyprexa Relprevv, Injections, and Alcohol

If you get the long-acting Zyprexa Relprevv injection, two points deserve attention.

First, the label describes a rare but serious reaction called **post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome**. In a small number of injections, more of the drug enters the bloodstream than intended, causing heavy sedation, confusion, slurred speech, dizziness, and in some cases loss of consciousness. Because of this, people are watched at a healthcare facility for at least three hours after each injection and are told not to drive or operate machinery for the rest of that day. Drinking on an injection day would make these symptoms worse and harder to recognize, so don't.

Second, as noted above, the injection gives you olanzapine continuously. Every day between injections counts as a day "on" the drug as far as alcohol is concerned.

The short-acting hospital injection is usually given in situations where alcohol isn't involved, but if someone who has been drinking heavily receives it, the medical team needs to know about the alcohol. Always tell clinicians if you've been drinking.

## Symbyax and Lybalvi: The Combination Forms

**Symbyax (olanzapine plus fluoxetine).** This pairs olanzapine with the antidepressant fluoxetine. Alcohol advice for fluoxetine on its own is also to avoid or limit drinking, because alcohol can worsen depression and add to side effects like drowsiness. On Symbyax you get both concerns at once. Our guide to [Prozac and alcohol](/never-hungover/prozac-and-alcohol) covers the fluoxetine side in more detail, and our broader guide to [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol) explains why alcohol and depression treatment work against each other.

**Lybalvi (olanzapine plus samidorphan).** Samidorphan blocks opioid receptors, which is why Lybalvi must not be used by people who take opioids or are in opioid withdrawal. The olanzapine part brings the same alcohol cautions as Zyprexa. If you take Lybalvi, ask your prescriber specifically about alcohol, and be open about any opioid pain medicine you use, since that's a separate serious issue.

## Don't Stop or Skip Olanzapine So You Can Drink

It's common to think, "I'll skip my dose this weekend so I can have a few drinks." With olanzapine, that tends to backfire.

- **The drug doesn't leave quickly.** With a half-life around 30 hours, skipping one dose barely lowers your levels by the evening. You'd still be combining them, while also missing your treatment.
- **Missing doses can let symptoms return.** For schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, consistent dosing is part of what keeps symptoms controlled. Missed doses plus the lost sleep that often comes with a night out is a known setup for a relapse of mania or psychosis.
- **Stopping suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms.** Official product information for olanzapine (the European label, for example) notes that stopping it abruptly has rarely been linked to symptoms such as sweating, trouble sleeping, shakiness, anxiety, nausea, and vomiting.

If you want to stop or reduce olanzapine, for any reason, plan it with your prescriber so it can be done gradually and safely. If you drank and aren't sure whether to take your next dose, call your prescriber, a pharmacist, or an after-hours nurse line rather than guessing. Never take an extra dose to "make up" for one you skipped.

## Alcohol, Mood, and the Conditions Olanzapine Treats

Beyond the direct drug interaction, alcohol can work against the reason you take olanzapine in the first place.

- **Bipolar disorder.** Alcohol can disrupt sleep and mood rhythms, and disrupted sleep is a well-known trigger for mood episodes. Drinking can also make mood swings harder to read for you and the people around you.
- **Schizophrenia and psychosis.** Alcohol can worsen symptoms for some people and makes it harder to tell which symptoms come from the illness, the medicine, or the alcohol.
- **Depression.** Alcohol is a depressant. Its mood lift is brief, and the low that follows can be worse, especially the next day.
- **Sleep.** Alcohol may help you fall asleep faster, but it breaks up sleep in the second half of the night. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the pattern.

None of this means you've done something wrong if you've had a drink. It means it's worth being honest with your prescriber about how much you drink, so they can factor it into your treatment.

## Weight, Blood Sugar, and Cholesterol: The Slower Interaction

Olanzapine is known for metabolic side effects. Its label warns about weight gain, high blood sugar (including new diabetes), and raised cholesterol and triglycerides, and doctors usually monitor weight, blood sugar, and blood fats while you take it. Among antipsychotics, olanzapine is one of those most strongly linked to these effects.

Alcohol adds to this picture over time:

- **Calories.** Drinks carry a lot of calories, and olanzapine already tends to increase appetite. Late-night food after drinking adds more.
- **Triglycerides.** Regular drinking can raise triglycerides, a type of blood fat that olanzapine can also raise.
- **Blood sugar.** Alcohol can swing blood sugar, and it can cause low blood sugar if you drink without eating. That matters more if olanzapine has affected your blood sugar control or if you take diabetes medicine.
- **Liver.** Olanzapine can raise liver enzymes in some people, and the label advises care in people with liver problems. Heavy drinking stresses the liver too. If your doctor checks your liver tests, mention how much you drink.

This interaction doesn't hit in one night. It builds over months, which is why it's easy to overlook.

## Heat, Dehydration, and Body Temperature

The olanzapine label warns that antipsychotics can interfere with the body's ability to lower its temperature. This matters when you're exercising hard, in hot weather, dehydrated, or taking other drugs with anticholinergic effects.

Alcohol dehydrates you and can dull your sense of being too hot. A summer festival, a long day in the sun, or a packed, hot bar is exactly the kind of setting where this adds up. Drink water alongside anything else, stay in the shade, take breaks, and pay attention to signs of overheating like a pounding headache, confusion, or feeling faint.

## Seizure Risk and Alcohol Withdrawal

Olanzapine, like other antipsychotics, carries a label caution about seizures, because it may lower the seizure threshold slightly. Heavy drinking followed by a sudden stop can also cause seizures as part of alcohol withdrawal.

This is a concern mainly for people who drink heavily every day, not for occasional social drinkers. But it's worth knowing the signs. If you drink a lot most days and you notice shaking, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, nausea, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there within a day or two of cutting back, that can be alcohol withdrawal. Don't push through it alone. Contact a doctor promptly, and call 911 for a seizure, confusion, or hallucinations. Withdrawal can be managed safely with medical help.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

> **Call 911 or get emergency care if someone on olanzapine has been drinking and:**
> - Is very hard to wake, or can't stay awake
> - Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or has bluish lips
> - Faints, collapses, or can't stand
> - Has a seizure
> - Is confused, disoriented, or agitated in a way that isn't normal for them
> - Has a high temperature with stiff muscles, heavy sweating, or a fast heartbeat (this can be a rare reaction called neuroleptic malignant syndrome)
> - Is vomiting while very drowsy (there's a risk of choking)
>
> While you wait for help, don't leave them alone, lay them on their side if they're drowsy or vomiting, and don't give them coffee, food, or more medicine.

**Call a doctor or pharmacist soon (not an emergency) if:**

- You feel unusually dizzy or lightheaded when you stand up after drinking
- You fell, even if you feel okay
- You're much drowsier the next day than usual
- You took an extra dose or aren't sure whether you did
- You notice your mood or symptoms changing after drinking

If you're unsure whether something is an emergency, US Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 can help 24 hours a day.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people face higher risk if olanzapine and alcohol are combined:

- **Older adults.** Falls, sedation, and blood pressure drops are more dangerous with age. The label also carries a boxed warning that elderly people with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have a higher risk of death, and olanzapine isn't approved for that use.
- **People who just started olanzapine or changed their dose.** Sedation and dizziness are usually strongest early on.
- **People taking other sedating medicines**, such as benzodiazepines, sleep pills, opioids, gabapentin, or sedating antihistamines.
- **People who drive or operate machinery** for work.
- **People with diabetes, heart disease, low blood pressure, liver problems, or a seizure history.**
- **People on the Relprevv injection**, especially on injection days.

A note on smoking: olanzapine is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme (CYP1A2) that cigarette smoke speeds up. That's why smokers often need different doses. If you only smoke when you drink, or you quit smoking, your olanzapine levels can shift, so let your prescriber know about changes in your smoking.

## How Olanzapine Compares With Other Antipsychotics and Alcohol

If you're comparing notes with someone on a different medicine, here's the general picture. All antipsychotics come with alcohol cautions, but the main risks differ with each drug's side-effect profile.

- **Quetiapine (Seroquel)** is also strongly sedating and lowers blood pressure on standing, so its alcohol concerns are similar. See our guide to [Seroquel and alcohol](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol).
- **Aripiprazole (Abilify)** tends to be less sedating, but alcohol still impairs judgment and coordination on top of it, and it carries its own impulse-control warnings. See [Abilify and alcohol](/never-hungover/abilify-and-alcohol).
- **Lithium**, often used alongside or instead of antipsychotics for bipolar disorder, has a different main concern: dehydration from alcohol can change lithium levels. See [lithium and alcohol](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol).

Olanzapine sits at the more sedating, more metabolic end of the group, which is why it gets some of the strictest advice.

## What About Hangover Supplements Like DHM?

If you take olanzapine, the key point is this: **talk to your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement that might affect the brain**, and that includes hangover products.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, and some of it shows DHM acting on the brain's GABA-A receptors, the same calming system that alcohol and many sedatives act on. There is no research on combining DHM with olanzapine, so nobody can tell you that stacking them is safe. There is also no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation, fall risk, or breathing risk of mixing olanzapine with alcohol. It does not make drinking on olanzapine safe.

If you take olanzapine, the safest plan is the one your prescriber agrees with, and no supplement changes how olanzapine and alcohol interact. For how other prescription medicines interact with alcohol, our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) summarizes the main drug classes, and our guides to [Seroquel and alcohol](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol) and [Abilify and alcohol](/never-hungover/abilify-and-alcohol) cover two other antipsychotics in the same family. If you don't take any prescription medicine and simply want to feel better after a night out, the habits with the best evidence are the plain ones in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover): drink less, drink slower, eat, and alternate with water.

## The Bottom Line

- The Zyprexa medication guide tells patients to avoid alcohol. The prescribing information reports that alcohol worsened olanzapine's drop in blood pressure on standing.
- The main risks are heavy drowsiness, dizziness, falls, accidents, impaired judgment, and at larger amounts, deep sedation and slowed breathing.
- Olanzapine's long half-life means spacing out a drink and a dose doesn't remove the interaction. The same goes for the long-acting injection.
- Don't skip or stop doses so you can drink. It barely lowers your levels and can let symptoms return.
- Over time, alcohol adds to olanzapine's effects on weight, blood sugar, and blood fats.
- If your prescriber hasn't said it's okay for you, don't drink. If someone on olanzapine is hard to wake or breathing slowly after drinking, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking olanzapine?**

The Zyprexa medication guide tells patients to avoid alcohol. Olanzapine and alcohol both sedate the brain, and the prescribing information reports that alcohol worsened olanzapine's drop in blood pressure on standing. Together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, falls, and impaired judgment, and at larger amounts slowed breathing. Some prescribers allow an occasional drink for a stable patient, but that's an individual decision. Ask yours before drinking at all.

**Is Zyprexa the same as olanzapine?**

Yes. Olanzapine is the generic name and Zyprexa is the original brand. Zyprexa Zydis (dissolving tablet), Zyprexa Relprevv (long-acting injection), Symbyax (with fluoxetine), and Lybalvi (with samidorphan) all contain olanzapine, and the alcohol warning applies to every form.

**How long after taking olanzapine can I drink?**

There's no safe waiting window if you take it regularly. Olanzapine's half-life averages around 30 hours, so daily dosing keeps fairly steady levels around the clock, and tablets peak roughly six hours after a dose. Spacing a drink away from your dose doesn't remove the interaction. Ask your prescriber what, if anything, is reasonable for you.

**What happens if you mix Zyprexa and alcohol?**

Most often, much stronger drowsiness, dizziness, clumsiness, and fuzzy thinking than either alone, plus a higher chance of fainting or falling when you stand. With more alcohol or other sedatives, it can lead to deep sedation and slowed breathing, which is an emergency. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, very confused, very hot and stiff, or having a seizure.

**Should I skip my olanzapine dose if I want to drink?**

No. Because olanzapine leaves the body slowly, skipping one dose barely lowers your levels, so you'd still be combining them while missing treatment. Missed doses can let symptoms of bipolar disorder or schizophrenia return. If you've been drinking and aren't sure about your next dose, call your prescriber or a pharmacist, and never double up later.

**Can I drink on the Zyprexa Relprevv injection?**

The injection releases olanzapine steadily for weeks, so the alcohol caution applies every day between shots. On injection days, the label requires at least three hours of observation because of a rare heavy-sedation reaction and says not to drive for the rest of the day. Don't drink on injection days, and ask your prescriber about alcohol in general.

**Does alcohol make olanzapine weight gain worse?**

It can add to it over time. Olanzapine commonly increases appetite and can raise weight, blood sugar, and triglycerides. Alcohol adds calories, can raise triglycerides, and often leads to late-night eating. If you drink regularly, tell your doctor so it can be considered alongside your metabolic monitoring.

**Can I take DHM or a hangover supplement while on olanzapine?**

Ask your prescriber or pharmacist first. DHM acts on GABA-A receptors in animal research, and there is no research on combining it with olanzapine. There is also no good evidence that DHM reduces the risks of mixing olanzapine and alcohol, so it does not make drinking on olanzapine safe.
